summary:
SARAN SHIFT is an evidence-traceable flood-investigation workflow built around NISAR Synthetic Aperture Radar observations near Saran, Bihar. It compares calibrated GCOV HH backscatter from 14 and 26 August 2026, expresses change in decibels, filters unreliable cells, and groups spatially connected high-change cells into inspectable candidate regions. A linked evidence explorer lets analysts compare before-and-after imagery, review thresholds, inspect connected components and signal profiles, check quality metadata, and trace results to source files.
The project addresses a core challenge in flood monitoring: flooding evolves over time, while radar-brightness changes can have several causes and cannot automatically be labeled as inundation. SARAN SHIFT therefore frames its output as a prioritized candidate for independent verification, not a confirmed flood map. This is important because it combines NISAR’s wide-area, all-weather sensing with transparent rules, geographic outputs, contextual hydrology reporting, and explicit uncertainty, helping analysts focus limited validation effort where it matters most.
details:
We developed NiSAR-Saran, an evidence-first Earth observation project that demonstrates how NISAR radar data can support local environmental monitoring. The project organizes satellite data, documents the processing workflow, compares consistent observations, produces geospatial outputs, and presents the results in a clear, reproducible format.

The workflow uses NISAR L2 GCOV H5 data, applies quality checks and spatial masks, calculates radar backscatter change, identifies areas that may require further investigation, and exports machine-readable summaries, point data, GeoJSON footprints, reports, and maps. The project also records the input data sources, timestamps, file hashes, processing assumptions, and limitations so another researcher can repeat the analysis.

Its benefits include transparent satellite-data interpretation, faster screening of areas of interest, better communication between technical and non-technical users, and a reusable structure for future environmental or disaster-monitoring studies. The intended impact is to help researchers, local authorities, and response teams use openly documented Earth observation methods to understand changing conditions and decide where additional validation is needed.

We developed the project on Ubuntu using Python, Bash, and Rust. Tools and libraries include h5py, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib, GeoPandas, Pyogrio, GeoJSON, Git, and standard Linux command-line tools. No specialized hardware was required beyond a regular Ubuntu workstation.

Our creativity lies in how we analyzed the NISAR data, not simply in presenting a map. We built a matched two-date comparison using the same track, frame, frequency, grid, and polarization. Instead of examining the brightest pixel, we used a scene-relative statistical threshold, grouped neighboring high-change cells into a connected candidate, and measured its footprint and location. We then checked the result using cross-polarization, another frequency, data masks, number of looks, sensitivity thresholds, and time-stamped external context. This layered approach turns a large radar dataset into a focused, testable research lead while keeping the interpretation open to further validation.
